lead: A stereo FM station must send two audio signals, left and right, on one carrier. It builds a composite baseband: the sum L + R in the ordinary audio band, so mono radios still work; a small 19 kHz pilot tone; and the difference L − R on a suppressed 38 kHz subcarrier. The receiver rebuilds the 38 kHz carrier from the pilot, detects the difference, and adds and subtracts to get L and R back. This chapter also follows the whole superheterodyne FM receiver from antenna to loudspeakers.
prereq: You need: DSB-SC and coherent detection, frequency division multiplexing and the superheterodyne receiver (see the units on amplitude modulation systems), and Pre-emphasis and de-emphasis.

blocks.text: Sending L and R on two carriers would double the spectrum, so the transmitter combines them into one baseband signal and frequency modulates the carrier with it. Stereo FM is frequency-division multiplexing done before the modulator.

Compatibility decides the layout. A mono receiver tuned to a stereo station must still sound right, so the sum L + R goes in the plain audio band, 0 to 15 kHz. A mono set low-pass filters its discriminator output at 15 kHz and plays L + R, the whole programme.

The difference L − R carries the stereo information. It modulates a 38 kHz subcarrier as DSB-SC, so it occupies 38 − 15 = 23 kHz to 38 + 15 = 53 kHz. The stereo baseband is therefore 0 to 53 kHz (Figure 3.8.1). Services above 53 kHz, such as RDS data at 57 kHz, are optional extras.
L and R are the left and right audio voltages; (L + R) comes from the 0–15 kHz band and (L − R) from the 38 kHz detector. This adding and subtracting is the matrix.

The difference channel is DSB-SC, which saves the power a 38 kHz carrier would take, but coherent detection needs a 38 kHz reference of the right phase. So the transmitter sends a small unmodulated tone at half that frequency, 19 kHz: the pilot. It sits in the empty gap between 15 kHz and 23 kHz and uses about 8 to 10 % of the total modulation.

The receiver filters out the pilot and doubles it with a phase-locked loop or a doubler: 2 × 19 = 38 kHz. The transmitter made its own 38 kHz subcarrier by doubling the same 19 kHz oscillator, so the receiver's 38 kHz is locked in phase to the suppressed carrier. A pilot at half the frequency also cannot be confused with anything in the L − R band, which starts at 23 kHz.

Phase matters. If the recovered 38 kHz is off by an angle φ, the synchronous detector delivers (L − R)cos φ instead of L − R. Then the left output becomes L(1 + cos φ)/2 + R(1 − cos φ)/2, and some right signal leaks into the left channel.
separation = 20 log[(1 + cos φ)/(1 − cos φ)] dB
φ is the phase error of the recovered 38 kHz subcarrier. φ = 10° gives 42.3 dB; φ = 30° gives 22.9 dB.
FM broadcasting uses 88 to 108 MHz with a peak deviation of 75 kHz. The receiver is a superheterodyne:

items: The RF amplifier selects the band, sets the noise figure and gives some image rejection.
The mixer with a local oscillator, usually f<sub>LO</sub> = f<sub>c</sub> + 10.7 MHz, moves the station to the 10.7 MHz intermediate frequency.
The IF amplifier, with a filter about 200 kHz wide, gives most of the gain and the selectivity.
The limiter strips amplitude changes, so noise that arrived as AM never reaches the detector.
The discriminator (ratio detector, quadrature detector or a digital equivalent) gives back the composite baseband.
The stereo decoder: a 19 kHz pilot filter and doubler, a synchronous detector for L − R, and the matrix.
De-emphasis on each output restores a flat response and cuts the treble noise; two audio amplifiers drive the loudspeakers.

blocks.text: Because the IF is 10.7 MHz, the image of a station lies 21.4 MHz above it, outside the 20 MHz wide FM band, so a modest RF filter rejects it. Stereo widens the signal: by Carson's rule a mono signal needs 2(75 + 15) = 180 kHz, but with the 53 kHz baseband it needs 2(75 + 53) = 256 kHz. Stations in one area are therefore kept several channels apart. De-emphasis must act on the separate outputs (or on L + R and L − R after detection), never on the composite, where it would crush the 23–53 kHz difference band and the pilot.

examples.question: A stereo FM transmitter is fed test tones of L = 1 V and R = 0.5 V peak. Find the matrix outputs, the bands present in the composite signal and its total width, and the signals the receiver recovers.
steps: Sum: L + R = 1 + 0.5 = 1.5 V. Difference: L − R = 1 − 0.5 = 0.5 V.
The sum occupies 0 to 15 kHz; a mono receiver plays only this.
The difference is DSB-SC on 38 kHz, so its sidebands span 23 to 53 kHz.
The pilot is at 19 kHz, between 15 and 23 kHz. The composite extends to 53 kHz.
The receiver doubles the pilot to 38 kHz, detects L − R = 0.5 V, and the matrix gives L = (1.5 + 0.5)/2 = 1.0 V and R = (1.5 − 0.5)/2 = 0.5 V, the inputs.
examples.answer: L + R = 1.5 V in 0–15 kHz, pilot at 19 kHz, L − R = 0.5 V in 23–53 kHz; composite 53 kHz wide; recovered L = 1.0 V, R = 0.5 V.

examples.question: A receiver is tuned to a 98.3 MHz stereo station with Δf = 75 kHz. Find the local oscillator frequency (high-side) and the image frequency, the Carson bandwidth in mono and in stereo, and the stereo separation if the recovered 38 kHz has a 10° phase error.
steps: Mono: B<sub>T</sub> = 2(75 + 15) = 180 kHz. Stereo: B<sub>T</sub> = 2(75 + 53) = 256 kHz.
examples.answer: f<sub>LO</sub> = 109.0 MHz, image 119.7 MHz; Carson 180 kHz mono and 256 kHz stereo; separation 42.3 dB.

traps: The pilot is 19 kHz and the subcarrier 38 kHz. The 38 kHz carrier itself is suppressed and never sent.
The difference channel is DSB-SC, not SSB and not FM. It needs both sidebands, 23 to 53 kHz.
A mono receiver loses nothing: it plays L + R, the full programme; its 15 kHz low-pass removes the pilot and the difference band.
A phase error in the recovered 38 kHz scales L − R by cos φ; it does not mix L + R into the difference channel.
The pilot and L − R share the 75 kHz peak deviation; they do not add to it. In Carson's rule use the highest baseband frequency, 53 kHz, for stereo.

quiz.q: State the pilot frequency, the subcarrier frequency, and the band of the difference channel.
quiz.a: Pilot 19 kHz; subcarrier 38 kHz, suppressed; difference channel 23 to 53 kHz.

quiz.q: Why is the difference sent as DSB-SC rather than with its 38 kHz carrier?
quiz.a: A 38 kHz carrier would take a large share of the 75 kHz deviation budget while carrying no information, leaving less for the programme. The audio would not hear it (it is far above 15 kHz), but the power would be wasted. A small 19 kHz pilot is enough to rebuild the carrier.

quiz.q: A stereo signal has L = 0.8 V and R = 0.2 V. Find the matrix outputs and the bands in the composite.
quiz.a: L + R = 1.0 V in 0–15 kHz; L − R = 0.6 V on 38 kHz in 23–53 kHz; pilot at 19 kHz. The composite extends to 53 kHz.

quiz.q: The recovered subcarrier has a 30° phase error. Find the stereo separation.
Why is the pilot at exactly half the subcarrier frequency rather than any convenient tone?
quiz.a: The receiver makes the subcarrier by doubling the pilot, and the transmitter made it by doubling the same oscillator, so the receiver's 38 kHz has the right frequency and phase. At 19 kHz the pilot also sits in an empty gap, clear of the 0–15 kHz and 23–53 kHz bands.

quiz.q: A stereo station sounds correct on an old mono radio. Explain why.
quiz.a: The mono radio low-pass filters at 15 kHz and plays L + R, the full programme. It ignores the pilot and the 23–53 kHz difference band, so it simply hears no stereo effect.

quiz.q: Give the FM broadcast band, the peak deviation and the usual IF.
quiz.a: 88–108 MHz, ±75 kHz peak deviation, 10.7 MHz IF.

beyond: Not for the exam. RDS data rides on a 57 kHz subcarrier locked to the third harmonic of the pilot; it is how a car radio shows the station name. Digital systems such as DAB+ and HD Radio carry coded audio instead. Modern stereo decoders are a few lines of DSP inside a software-defined radio, with the pilot recovered by a phase-locked loop. Search for FM composite baseband, MPX power and RDS.

figure.caption: The composite baseband of worked example 1. L + R fills 0 to 15 kHz, the 19 kHz pilot sits in the gap, and L − R rides as two sidebands around a suppressed 38 kHz carrier from 23 to 53 kHz; RDS, where used, sits at 57 kHz.
